lesson_title: The Month Written Down Before It Happens: Budgeting
hook_text: She saved R800 on advertising — and it cost her R3 600. The cheapest line on the budget was the most expensive thing she bought.
clip_script: Nolwazi runs a weekend catering business, and at the end of every month she does something her neighbours call fussy: she writes down NEXT month before it happens. Two lists. Will the business make a profit — orders, ingredients, even the slow wearing of her big pots? And the harder list: will there be money in the account on the RIGHT DAYS? Because school fees want the third, the taxi association wants the first, and the wedding client only pays on the twenty-sixth. Profitable and broke are different things — bills arrive on dates, not averages. Then month-end comes, and she sits with two columns: planned, and happened. Orders: planned twenty thousand, actual sixteen four. Down three thousand six hundred — why? Her eye catches the next line. Flyers and boosted posts: planned eight hundred. Spent: nothing. She skipped the advertising to save money. There is the answer, staring back in two rows: she saved eight hundred rand and lost three thousand six hundred in orders. The saving was the most expensive thing she bought all month. That is the whole discipline of budgeting: write it down before, compare it after, and judge lines in PAIRS — because an underspend is not a victory until you know what the money was supposed to cause.
visual_style: A kitchen table at night, two handwritten columns glowing side by side; coins sliding between an advertising line and an orders line to show the causal pair; a calendar with bill dates lighting up in sequence.
mood: Intimate, practical, sharply illuminating at the reveal.
pacing: Quiet domestic open, calendar urgency in the middle, slow two-row reveal, firm closing rule.
